grn.name: Green

ind.name: Independent

bank.q: The US should have government-guaranteed healthcare for all, even if it means higher taxes.
bank.ctx: This supports a single, government-guaranteed health system funded by taxes so everyone is covered — the idea behind 'Medicare for All', championed by Bernie Sanders. The US is the only rich country without universal coverage, and medical bills are a leading cause of personal bankruptcy. The stake is whether healthcare is a right or a product you buy.

bank.q: Government-run healthcare means rationing and lost freedom; the private system should stay.
bank.ctx: This defends America's mainly private, insurance-based system, warning that a government takeover would mean rationing, waiting lists, and less choice and innovation. Supporters point to the US leading in new drugs and specialist care. The stake is whether the state or the market should run something as vital as health.

bank.q: Illegal immigration is an invasion that must be stopped with mass deportations and a border wall.
bank.ctx: This is a hardline border stance: treating illegal immigration as an 'invasion' to be stopped by mass deportation and a border wall, as Donald Trump has pledged. Around 11 million people live in the US without legal status. The stake is how far a country should go to enforce its borders.

bank.q: Immigrants, documented or not, are part of America, and mass deportation is cruel and un-American.
bank.ctx: This is the pro-immigrant view: that undocumented people — many of whom have lived and worked in the US for decades and have citizen children — are part of American society, and that mass deportation would be cruel, costly, and economically damaging. The stake is how a nation of immigrants treats those without papers.

bank.q: Undocumented immigrants who have lived here for years should get a path to citizenship.
bank.ctx: This supports a 'path to citizenship': letting undocumented immigrants who have lived and worked in the US for years earn legal status. Reagan's 1986 amnesty did this for about three million people; the 'Dreamers' debate concerns those brought as children. The stake is whether long-settled residents should be legalised or removed.

bank.q: Rewarding people who broke the law with citizenship just encourages more illegal immigration.
bank.ctx: This opposes an amnesty, arguing that rewarding people who broke immigration law encourages more illegal crossings — a 'magnet' effect. Supporters want enforcement first. The stake is whether legalising the undocumented is fair to legal immigrants and a deterrent or an incentive.

bank.q: Abortion is a fundamental right, and overturning Roe v. Wade was a grave injustice.
bank.ctx: This is the pro-choice position. Roe v. Wade was the 1973 Supreme Court ruling that made abortion a nationwide right until the Court overturned it in 2022, letting states ban it — which many did. The argument centres on a woman's control over her own body. The stake is who decides: the woman or the state.

bank.q: Abortion is the taking of an innocent life, and states are right to restrict or ban it.
bank.ctx: This is the pro-life position: that a foetus is a human life, so abortion takes a life and states are right to restrict or ban it now that Roe v. Wade is gone. It is rooted in Catholic and evangelical teaching and drove the decades-long campaign against Roe. The stake is the moral status of the unborn.

bank.q: The Second Amendment is nearly absolute; gun ownership should not be restricted.
bank.ctx: The Second Amendment protects the right to bear arms, and this treats it as nearly absolute. The US has more guns than people, and courts have expanded gun rights. Supporters see private firearms as both a constitutional right and a check on tyranny. The stake is where that right meets public safety.

bank.q: America’s gun bloodshed demands real restrictions, including bans on assault-style weapons.
bank.ctx: This is the gun-control case: that America's uniquely high rate of gun deaths and mass shootings — in schools, churches, and stores — demands real limits like banning assault-style rifles. Supporters point to far lower gun-death rates in countries with strict laws. The stake is how many restrictions the Second Amendment should allow.

bank.q: Donald Trump is a threat to American democracy.
bank.ctx: This holds that Donald Trump endangers American democracy — a widespread view among his critics, sharpened by his attempt to overturn the 2020 election result and the January 6th 2021 Capitol riot. The stake is whether Trump is a normal politician or a threat to democratic norms.

bank.q: The real threat to democracy is a establishment that weaponizes the courts against Trump and his voters.
bank.ctx: This is the pro-Trump counter-view: that the real danger comes from a political and legal 'establishment' that has weaponised prosecutions and the courts against Trump and, by extension, his tens of millions of voters. The stake is whether the many criminal cases against Trump are justice or persecution.

bank.q: The ultra-wealthy and big corporations should pay far more in taxes.
bank.ctx: This supports much higher taxes on the ultra-wealthy and big corporations to fund public services and curb inequality, echoing proposals from Sanders and Elizabeth Warren for wealth taxes. US inequality is near its highest in a century. The stake is whether the rich pay their 'fair share'.

bank.q: Raising taxes on job creators and businesses just kills investment and growth.
bank.ctx: This opposes higher taxes on the wealthy and business, arguing they are the 'job creators' whose investment drives growth, and that heavy taxes push capital and companies offshore. It reflects supply-side ('trickle-down') economics. The stake is whether taxing the top helps or harms everyone else.

bank.q: Climate change is a crisis, and the US must transform its economy to fight it.
bank.ctx: This treats climate change as a crisis requiring rapid, sweeping change to the US economy — the thinking behind the Green New Deal and the Biden-era clean-energy law. Scientists warn of worsening heat, fires, and storms. The stake is how much economic disruption is worth accepting to cut emissions.

bank.q: Climate alarmism is being used to justify a costly government takeover of the economy.
bank.ctx: This is climate-policy scepticism: that 'alarmism' is exaggerated and used to justify costly government control over energy and the economy, hitting ordinary families with higher bills for little gain while China keeps emitting. The stake is whether aggressive climate policy is prudent or self-harming.

bank.q: Systemic racism is real and America must take active steps to address it.
bank.ctx: 'Systemic racism' means discrimination built into institutions — policing, housing, hiring — rather than just individual prejudice. This holds it is real and must be actively addressed, the view behind Black Lives Matter and DEI programs. The stake is whether racial inequality today is mainly structural.

bank.q: The obsession with systemic racism is itself divisive and teaches Americans to see race everywhere.
bank.ctx: This pushes back on the systemic-racism framework, arguing that constantly foregrounding race is itself divisive, teaches people to see everything through a racial lens, and downplays how far America has progressed. It reflects opposition to 'critical race theory' in schools. The stake is how to think about race in modern America.

bank.q: Some races are simply more intelligent or capable than others.
bank.ctx: This is a statement of racial supremacism — the belief that some races are innately more intelligent or capable than others. It was the ideological engine of Nazism and the Holocaust, and of systems like slavery and apartheid. Modern genetics finds more variation within any racial group than between them, and the idea has no scientific standing.

bank.q: There is no hierarchy of races; the idea is pseudo-science with a shameful history.
bank.ctx: This states the principle of fundamental human equality: that no race is innately superior in intelligence or ability, and that racial hierarchies are discredited pseudo-science with a shameful history behind slavery and apartheid. It is the moral baseline of modern anti-discrimination law.

bank.q: The answer to crime is more police and tougher sentences, not less.
bank.ctx: This favours a tough-on-crime approach — more police, longer sentences — echoing the 1990s 'three strikes' era. Supporters point to crime spikes and argue dangerous offenders belong behind bars. The US already jails a larger share of its people than any nation. The stake is whether more policing and prison make people safer.

bank.q: Mass incarceration and aggressive policing have failed; the money should go to prevention.
bank.ctx: This argues America's experiment with mass incarceration and aggressive policing failed — it locked up millions without proportionate safety gains — and that money should shift to prevention, mental health, and addiction. It reflects criminal-justice reform and 'defund' debates. The stake is what actually reduces crime.

bank.q: Trans Americans should be able to change their legal gender and access gender-affirming care.
bank.ctx: This supports letting trans Americans change their legal gender and access gender-affirming care such as hormones. It is a flashpoint in US 'culture war' politics, especially over care for minors. The stake is how the law and medicine should treat gender identity.

bank.q: Biological sex is real, and children especially should not be pushed toward gender transition.
bank.ctx: This is the gender-critical view: that biological sex is real and fixed, and that children especially should not be steered toward medical transition, given debate over its long-term effects. Several US states have restricted youth care. The stake is the balance between trans rights and caution, particularly for minors.

bank.q: The federal minimum wage should be raised to at least 15 dollars an hour.
bank.ctx: The federal minimum wage has been stuck at $7.25 an hour since 2009. This supports raising it to at least $15, as the 'Fight for $15' movement demands, arguing full-time work should lift people out of poverty. The stake is whether a wage floor should guarantee a living.

bank.q: Forcing wages up by law just closes small businesses and destroys entry-level jobs.
bank.ctx: This opposes a large minimum-wage rise, arguing that forcing pay above what a job produces leads employers to cut hours, automate, or close — hurting the very low-skilled workers it aims to help. The stake is whether higher minimums lift workers or cost them jobs.

bank.q: Student debt is crushing a generation and much of it should be cancelled.
bank.ctx: Americans owe over $1.7 trillion in student loans, and this supports cancelling much of it, as Biden attempted before the courts blocked parts. Supporters say the debt crushes a generation's ability to buy homes or start families. The stake is whether that debt is a public burden to relieve.

bank.q: Cancelling student debt forces people who never went to college to pay for those who did.
bank.ctx: This opposes student-debt cancellation as unfair: it makes taxpayers who never went to college, or who repaid their loans, foot the bill for those who borrowed — often for degrees that raise their earnings. The stake is who should bear the cost of higher education.

bank.q: Programs like Social Security and Medicare should be expanded, not cut.
bank.ctx: Social Security (pensions) and Medicare (elderly healthcare) are huge, popular federal programs that tens of millions rely on. This supports expanding rather than cutting them. Both face long-term funding gaps as the population ages. The stake is how America keeps its promises to older citizens.

bank.q: Entitlement spending is bankrupting the country and must be reined in.
bank.ctx: This warns that spending on these 'entitlements', which dominate the federal budget, is driving an unsustainable national debt and must be reined in — for instance by raising the retirement age. The stake is balancing support for the elderly against long-term solvency.

bank.q: The US should keep arming Ukraine against Russia for as long as it takes.
bank.ctx: This supports continuing US military and financial aid to Ukraine against Russia's 2022 invasion, for as long as it takes. Supporters argue letting Russia win would embolden aggressors and endanger NATO allies. The stake is America's role in defending Ukraine.

bank.q: Endless funding for foreign wars is money that should be spent on Americans at home.
bank.ctx: This opposes open-ended funding for the war, an 'America First' argument that the tens of billions sent to Ukraine should be spent on Americans at home and that the US should not be the world's policeman. The stake is how far US interests extend abroad.

bank.q: The US should continue its strong military and financial support for Israel.
bank.ctx: This supports continued strong US military and financial backing for Israel, a long-standing ally, especially amid its war in Gaza. Supporters cite shared democratic values and strategic interest. The stake is the depth of America's commitment to Israel.

bank.q: The US should stop bankrolling Israel and condition or end its military aid.
bank.ctx: This wants the US to condition or end military aid to Israel, a view that grew on the left over the civilian toll in Gaza. Supporters argue American weapons should not enable what they see as disproportionate harm. The stake is whether US support for Israel should be unconditional.

bank.q: Tariffs to protect American industry and jobs are worth the higher prices.
bank.ctx: Tariffs are taxes on imported goods. This backs using them to protect American factories and jobs from cheaper foreign competition, even if it raises prices — the logic behind Trump's tariffs on China and others. The stake is whether protecting industry is worth costlier goods.

bank.q: Tariffs are a tax on American families and start trade wars that hurt everyone.
bank.ctx: This opposes tariffs, arguing they are really a tax on American families through higher prices, and that they provoke retaliatory trade wars that hurt US farmers and exporters. Most economists share this view. The stake is whether tariffs help or harm the wider economy.

bank.q: America is a Christian nation and its laws should reflect Christian values.
bank.ctx: This is Christian nationalism: the belief that America is fundamentally a Christian nation whose laws should reflect Christian values, on issues from abortion to school prayer. Supporters see faith as the nation's moral foundation. The stake is the role of religion in American law.

bank.q: The separation of church and state is fundamental; religion has no place in law.
bank.ctx: This defends the separation of church and state, a founding US principle in the First Amendment, keeping government neutral on religion so no faith is imposed on a diverse population. The stake is whether law should rest on religious doctrine or secular reasoning.

bank.q: Islam is not compatible with American values.
bank.ctx: This argues Islam clashes with American values on issues like free speech and women's rights — a view that fuelled support for measures like Trump's 2017 'travel ban'. Critics call it prejudice against a diverse faith of millions of Americans. The stake is whether the concern is about security or bigotry.

bank.q: Muslim Americans are full citizens, and their faith deserves the same respect as any other.
bank.ctx: This holds that Muslim Americans are full and equal citizens whose faith deserves the same respect and protection as any other under the Constitution. The stake is religious equality versus singling out one faith.

bank.q: Free speech is under threat from cancel culture and campus censorship.
bank.ctx: 'Cancel culture' refers to people losing jobs or being publicly shamed over their opinions, especially on campuses. This argues free speech is genuinely under threat from this and from ideological conformity. Supporters span left and right libertarians. The stake is whether open debate is being chilled.

bank.q: The free-speech panic is overblown cover for people who just want to say bigoted things without consequences.
bank.ctx: This argues the free-speech panic is overblown and often a shield for people who want to voice bigotry without criticism — that facing social consequences for what you say is not censorship. The stake is the line between free speech and accountability for it.

bank.q: Diversity, equity, and inclusion programs have gone too far and should be scrapped.
bank.ctx: DEI — Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion — refers to workplace and campus programs to boost underrepresented groups. This argues they have overreached, become box-ticking or ideological, and should be scrapped, as several states and companies have begun doing. The stake is whether such programs fix bias or create it.

bank.q: DEI programs exist because discrimination is real, and scrapping them just protects the powerful.
bank.ctx: This defends DEI as a response to real, documented discrimination in hiring and promotion, arguing that scrapping it mainly protects those who already hold advantages. The stake is whether deliberate inclusion efforts are fair correction or unfair preference.

bank.q: Marijuana should be legal nationwide and drug use treated as a health issue.
bank.ctx: This supports legalising marijuana nationwide — already legal in many states — and treating drug use as a health issue, not a crime, to cut the harms of the 'war on drugs' and mass incarceration. The stake is whether prohibition or regulation better handles drugs.

bank.q: Loosening drug laws has fueled addiction and disorder, and it should be reversed.
bank.ctx: This argues loosening drug laws has fuelled addiction, homelessness, and public disorder — pointing to open-air drug scenes in some liberal cities — and should be reversed. The stake is whether a permissive approach helps users or worsens the crisis.

bank.q: Terminally ill adults should have the legal right to medically assisted death.
bank.ctx: 'Medically assisted death' lets terminally ill adults end their lives with a doctor's help, legal in states like Oregon and California under strict rules. This supports it as a compassionate right over one's own death. The stake is control over the end of life.

bank.q: Assisted dying puts pressure on the vulnerable and crosses a line society should not cross.
bank.ctx: This opposes assisted dying, warning it can pressure the elderly, disabled, or depressed toward death and crosses a line by involving doctors in ending life. The stake is whether the right to die risks the vulnerable being pushed toward it.

bank.q: Protecting the environment should take priority over expanding oil, gas, and coal.
bank.ctx: This puts protecting the environment ahead of expanding oil, gas, and coal — favouring limits on drilling and pipelines to cut emissions and safeguard land and water. The stake is the balance between conservation and fossil-fuel production.

bank.q: Energy independence and cheap power matter more than blocking drilling and pipelines.
bank.ctx: This prioritises cheap, home-produced energy and 'energy independence' over environmental restrictions, arguing US oil and gas keep prices low and reduce reliance on hostile states. The stake is whether energy security or climate should drive policy.

bank.q: Government should intervene heavily to make housing affordable, including rent control.
bank.ctx: This supports strong government action on housing costs, including rent control (legal caps on rent rises), as cities like New York use. Supporters say the market has failed ordinary renters. The stake is how far government should intervene in housing.

bank.q: Rent control and mandates make the housing shortage worse; deregulation lets the market build.
bank.ctx: This argues rent control and building mandates backfire — discouraging construction and worsening shortages — and that cutting zoning and permit red tape to let builders build is the real fix. Most economists are sceptical of rent control. The stake is whether regulation or deregulation solves the shortage.

bank.q: The Electoral College should be abolished in favor of the national popular vote.
bank.ctx: The Electoral College can hand the presidency to a candidate who loses the national popular vote, as happened in 2000 and 2016 (both won by Republicans). This wants it abolished so the most-voted candidate wins. The stake is how America chooses its president.

bank.q: The Electoral College protects smaller states and should be kept.
bank.ctx: This defends the Electoral College, arguing it forces candidates to build broad geographic coalitions and protects smaller and rural states from being ignored by big-city majorities. The stake is whether the system unfairly distorts votes or usefully balances regions.

bank.q: Universal background checks and red-flag laws are common-sense and should be federal law.
bank.ctx: This supports federal gun-safety measures: universal background checks on buyers and 'red-flag' laws letting courts temporarily remove guns from people deemed dangerous. Polls show broad support even among gun owners. The stake is finding limits compatible with gun rights.

bank.q: Background-check and red-flag schemes are a slippery slope to confiscation and should be resisted.
bank.ctx: This opposes those measures as a 'slippery slope' toward registration and eventual confiscation, arguing checks and red-flag laws burden the law-abiding without stopping criminals. The stake is whether such rules are common sense or the thin end of a wedge.

bank.q: Big Tech and monopolies should be broken up and tightly regulated.
bank.ctx: This supports breaking up and tightly regulating 'Big Tech' giants like Google, Amazon, and Meta, and other monopolies, on the grounds that their dominance harms competition, privacy, and democracy. It has support on both left and populist right. The stake is curbing corporate power.

bank.q: Heavy-handed regulation of successful companies just kills the innovation that made America rich.
bank.ctx: This argues heavy-handed regulation of successful companies kills the innovation and dynamism that made America's economy the world's most powerful, and that today's giants can be displaced by tomorrow's startups. The stake is whether antitrust action protects or stifles the economy.

bank.q: The US spends too much on its military and should cut the defense budget.
bank.ctx: The US spends more on its military than the next several countries combined. This argues that is excessive and the defense budget should be cut to fund domestic needs. The stake is whether America over-invests in its armed forces.

bank.q: A strong, well-funded military is what keeps America and its allies safe.
bank.ctx: This defends high military spending as what underwrites American and allied security and deters rivals like China and Russia. Supporters see strength as the guarantor of peace. The stake is whether that spending buys safety or crowds out other priorities.

bank.q: Children should be taught pride in America’s history, not mainly its sins.
bank.ctx: This favours patriotic education — teaching pride in America's founding and achievements rather than dwelling on its sins — the impulse behind Trump's '1776 Commission'. The stake is whether schools should build national pride or foreground historical wrongs.

bank.q: A country that hides slavery and its other crimes from students is lying to them.
bank.ctx: This supports teaching the hard parts of US history — slavery, segregation, treatment of Native Americans — arguing that hiding them, as fights over 'critical race theory' and banned books suggest, misleads students. The stake is honesty versus comfort in the classroom.

bank.q: Birthright citizenship for children born on US soil should be ended.
bank.ctx: Birthright citizenship — automatic citizenship for anyone born on US soil — comes from the 14th Amendment. This wants it ended, arguing it draws 'birth tourism' and rewards illegal entry. The stake is a change that would require altering or reinterpreting the Constitution.

bank.q: Birthright citizenship is in the Constitution and a core American principle that must be protected.
bank.ctx: This defends birthright citizenship as a constitutional guarantee and a defining American principle that has helped integrate generations of immigrants. The stake is whether a core 14th-Amendment right should be preserved.

bank.q: The poor and unemployed face too many hurdles; the safety net should be stronger and easier to access.
bank.ctx: This argues the poor and unemployed face too many hurdles — paperwork, work tests, benefit cliffs — and that the safety net should be stronger and easier to access. It reflects support for expanded aid like the pandemic-era child tax credit. The stake is how generous and accessible welfare should be.

bank.q: Welfare too easily becomes a trap, and work requirements protect taxpayers who fund it.
bank.ctx: This argues welfare can trap people in dependency and that work requirements, like those in the 1996 reform, protect the taxpayers who fund it and encourage self-reliance. The stake is whether conditions on aid help recipients or punish them.

bank.q: Long-standing traditions carry the wisdom of generations and should not be discarded lightly.
bank.ctx: This is the conservative philosophy of tradition, associated with Edmund Burke: that long-standing customs and institutions hold the accumulated, hard-won wisdom of generations, so change should be gradual and cautious rather than sweeping away what works for untested ideas.

bank.q: Worshipping tradition just lets the dead govern the living and blocks necessary change.
bank.ctx: This is the progressive reply, in the spirit of Thomas Paine's line that 'the dead should not govern the living': that treating tradition as sacred just lets the prejudices of the past block overdue reform — as appeals to tradition once defended slavery and denying women the vote.

bank.q: A good society depends more on personal responsibility than on government help.
bank.ctx: This reflects a core right-leaning value: that a healthy society depends mainly on individuals taking responsibility for their own choices and lives, and that leaning too heavily on government breeds dependence and saps initiative.

bank.q: Blaming individuals for problems the system creates is how the comfortable excuse others’ suffering.
bank.ctx: This reflects a core left-leaning value: that many hardships — poverty, poor health, joblessness — stem from unfair systems and circumstances beyond personal control, so blaming individuals lets the comfortable ignore problems they benefit from or could help fix.

heroSub: 70 statements on the issues defining America right now: healthcare, immigration, abortion, guns, and the economy. Every position is asked twice with opposite framing, revealing both your party alignment and your framing bias.

context:
Politics in the United States: the landscape behind this test

The United States runs a presidential system with a strict separation of powers and, in almost all federal races, first-past-the-post voting in single-member districts. That combination reliably produces two dominant parties. Third parties such as the Libertarians and the Greens shape debate and occasionally affect margins, but rarely win federal office.

The two-party structure

The Democratic and Republican parties are better understood as broad coalitions than as disciplined programmatic parties. Each contains factions that would be separate parties under proportional representation. The Democratic coalition spans moderates focused on incremental reform and a progressive wing pushing structural redistribution. The Republican coalition spans business-oriented conservatives, religious conservatives, and a nationalist-populist current that has reshaped the party since 2016.

Primaries matter enormously as a result. Because most districts are safe for one party, the contest that decides the seat is often the primary rather than the general election, which rewards candidates who appeal to the most committed voters.

The cleavages that actually divide voters

American politics is unusual among rich democracies in how tightly social and cultural questions bind to partisanship. Abortion, gun ownership, immigration, race, and religion predict party identification more strongly than income does. Healthcare remains genuinely contested in a way it is not in most of Europe, because the United States is the only wealthy democracy without universal coverage.

Education has become one of the sharpest dividing lines. College-educated voters have moved toward the Democrats while non-college voters, especially outside metropolitan areas, have moved toward the Republicans, partly reversing the older class alignment.

How this maps onto the compass

Both major parties sit to the economic right of their European counterparts. A position that reads as mainstream social democracy in Sweden reads as the left edge of the Democratic Party in the United States. On the governance axis the parties do not divide cleanly: each supports state authority in some domains and resists it in others.

This test asks about concrete American policy rather than abstractions, then reports how closely you align with each party. For the full profiles, see the US party guides.
